jsonld.name: Fish Tagine Chermoula

The Atlantic coast from Casablanca to Essaouira argues the fish (bream, sea bass, sardines; the list is the day's catch), and the chermoula (#93, this site's own record) is the constant.

skeleton:
Fish Tagine Chermoula

Moroccan · Medium · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The coast's tagine is built on chermoula twice: whole fish or thick steaks marinated in the herb-citrus paste, then laid on a bed of potatoes, tomatoes, and peppers — each slice also painted with the chermoula — and steamed gently in the tagine's own perfume until the vegetables become the sauce and the fish arrives at the table barely held together by its own tenderness. The Atlantic coast from Casablanca to Essaouira argues the fish (bream, sea bass, sardines; the list is the day's catch), and the chermoula (#93, this site's own record) is the constant.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

- **Marinate the fish 1 hour — the chermoula's longest honest duty.** The scored flesh drinks the marinade deeply; the half held back paints the vegetable bed. The chermoula's two-moments law (#93's own note) runs this dish at full scale: the marinade's depth inward, the reserved sauce's brightness outward. - **The bridge:** the fish is the coast's choice — any firm whole fish or steak runs the doctrine truly; the sardine version (#51's meatballs' cousin) is the resourceful small-fish seat. The potatoes run the base honestly; fennel fronds or thin fennel bulbs are the Atlantic coast's own addition.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The marinate: an hour, the scores drunk with chermoula.
  • The bed: layered and painted, the potatoes the floor, the water at the side.
  • The steam: the gentlest murmur, the fish at the bone's pull, the raw sauce at the end.

Fish Tagine Chermoula

Prep: 35 minutes, plus 1 hour marinating · Cook: 35 minutes · Total: About 2 hours 15 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 1 whole fish (about 1.2 kg — bream, sea bass, or snapper), cleaned, scaled, scored three times a side; or 4 thick steaks (about 200 g each)
  • 1 full recipe chermoula (#93) — or the quick build: 2 fists cilantro (about 40 g), 6 cloves garlic (about 25 g), 2 tsp cumin, 1 tsp paprika, ½ tsp saffron water (#120's steep), the juice of 1½ lemons (about 45 ml), 5 tbsp olive oil (about 65 g), salt — half for the fish, half for the vegetables
  • 3 potatoes (about 400 g), sliced to 5 mm rounds; 3 tomatoes (about 300 g), sliced thick
  • 1 onion (about 150 g), sliced to rings; 1 green or red pepper (about 120 g), sliced in rings; a handful of green olives (about 80 g)
  • 2 preserved lemon peels (#92), sliced to threads; a fist of cilantro (about 15 g) at the end
  • 100 ml water (about 100 g)

Instructions

  1. **Build the vegetable bed (10 minutes).** In the tagine or wide heavy pot, layer the potato rounds as the base's floor, the onion and pepper rings over them, the tomato slices last — each layer painted with strokes of the reserved chermoula as it is laid. The water poured gently down the pot's side. Checkpoint — the bed should be level and generous — the fish steams upon it, and the vegetables (the sauce's future) want the even depth. Taste a tomato slice: the chermoula's paint should be distinctly on it; the bed is seasoned layer by layer.
  2. **The fish's steam (25–30 minutes at the gentlest tremble).** Lay the marinated fish on the bed, pour its marinade's remains over, the olives and the preserved lemon threads around, and cover. Cook at the barest simmer — the pot's faintest murmur, roughly 90 °C at the surface — 25 minutes for steaks, 30 for a whole fish, until the flesh at the thickest score pulls at the bone's nudge and the vegetables have collapsed into a chermoula-perfumed, spoonable bed beneath. Checkpoint — the fish's doneness at the bone: the flesh opaque and just-parting at the score's depth — the pull test at the thickest point, not the clock's guess. The bed beneath: the potatoes tender to the fork, the tomatoes melted, the whole carrying chermoula's green through the steam's perfume. Do not over: a fish tagine held past its moment falls to the pot (a good fallen dish, but not the one intended).
  3. **The finish — bright, never cooked.** Off the heat: the remaining reserved chermoula spooned over the fish's back (the raw sauce's fire, the two-moments law's close), the fresh cilantro scattered, and the pot rested 5 minutes before the table. Checkpoint — eating test, with bread or the #34 couscous: the fish's silk over the vegetable bed's perfume — the chermoula's herb-garlic-citrus running through every element, the preserved lemon's salt-bitter thread and the olives' brine between — and the raw sauce's finish over the steamed, the two registers meeting only in the mouth. It should taste like the Atlantic's tagine: the day's fish, the coast's marinade, and the pot's gentlest steam.

Finish & Plate

The tagine to the table's center — the fish on its bed, the raw chermoula's green over its back, the lemon threads and olives visible — bread at every hand, and the pot's own serving as the ceremony.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Fish fell to the potOver-steamed or held past the pullThe bone's-pull test, not the clock
Bed watery, no sauceWater over-poured or under-steamedThe scant 100 ml; the potatoes are the binder
Chermoula perfume absentThe raw sauce skipped at the endThe two-moments law — the raw sauce is the voice

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The fish is served the hour (the reheated fish tagine is a lesser thing; the fallen pot becomes the next day's chermoula-flavored sauce for rice). The chermoula keeps 3 days; the vegetable bed's leftovers are the cook's own prize. - Variations: the sardine version, the #51 meatballs' chermoula seat, the fennel-fringed Atlantic build. The #93 chermoula and the #92 preserved lemons are this record's pantry parents.
